modules.title: Product analytics & research synthesis
modules.subtitle: Move from data to decisions through reproducible evidence.
objectives: Analyze structured data with traceable calculations.
Translate verified findings into decisions and stories.

slides.title: Begin with the business question
slides.takeaway: A chart should answer something worth deciding.
points: What happened, for whom, and in which period?
Which metric and comparison are appropriate?
What action could the result support?
slides.note: AI can assist with cleaning, analysis and communication. Its ability to inspect data depends on file access and calculation tools.

paragraphs: Start analytics with a decision question. Identify who or what you are measuring, the period, the comparison, and what action the result could inform. This keeps chart creation connected to product work.
For SkillForge, we might ask whether an acquisition channel brings learners who activate and complete the capstone at an acceptable cost. Paid-seat volume alone does not answer that question.
What is the decision behind the chart you want to make? State it before choosing the visualization.
Next, we will inspect the dataset and its definitions.

slides.title: Inspect before you interpret
slides.takeaway: Understand the data contract before plotting.
points: Check units, definitions, sheets and periods.
Inspect missing values, duplicates and filters.
Preserve notes, revisions and sample limitations.
slides.note: Filling missing values is an analytical choice, not an automatic improvement. Keep transformations explicit and retain the original dataset.

paragraphs: Before interpreting data, inspect its contract. Confirm units, date fields, event definitions, missing values, duplicates, and transformations. Data cleaning is an analytical choice, so record what changed and why.

In SkillForge's fictional funnel dataset, paid seats, activated learners, completed capstones, refunds, and marketing spend have different meanings. The exercise assumes each cohort has finished its eight-week window.
Which field could be misunderstood, and what definition would prevent that mistake? Check that the denominators are consistent.
Now we will answer two complementary chart questions.

slides.title: Two charts for a course business
slides.takeaway: Acquisition and learning success must be read together.
points: Paid enrollments by acquisition channel.
Paid, activated and completed learners by cohort month.
Funnel denominators and refund-adjusted tuition.
slides.note: The included Jan–Mar 2026 dataset is entirely fictional and assumes each cohort has finished its eight-week window. Do not compare immature and mature completion rates or infer real demand from the exercise.

paragraphs: Read acquisition and learning success together. One chart can compare paid enrollments by channel; another can compare paid, activated, and completed learners across mature cohorts. Keep the tables behind both charts available for verification.

The SkillForge lab lets you filter a channel and inspect its totals. The second chart deliberately shows all channels, as labeled. Net tuition subtracts fully refunded seats before multiplying by the assumed tuition.
Recalculate one total yourself. Then ask whether the observed pattern could reflect channel mix or cohort maturity rather than a product improvement.
Next, we will separate observation from explanation and action.

slides.title: Observation → explanation → decision
slides.takeaway: Do not skip the uncertainty in the middle.
points: Observation: what the data actually shows.
Hypothesis: a possible reason to investigate.
Decision: an action with a measurement plan.
slides.note: A rise in enrollment may reflect spend or channel mix rather than better positioning. Check whether activation, capstone completion, refunds and contribution move in a healthy direction.

paragraphs: An observation states what the data shows. An explanation is a hypothesis about why it happened. A decision is an action supported by that evidence and the uncertainty that remains. Keeping these separate prevents a chart from making a causal claim it cannot support.

If SkillForge has more paid seats in March than January, marketing spend, audience mix, timing, or positioning could explain it. We need a suitable comparison or experiment before crediting a particular feature.
Write one observation without using the word 'because.' Then write two possible explanations.
Now we will apply a similar evidence discipline to interview transcripts.

slides.title: Unstructured data needs traceability
slides.takeaway: Themes should point back to actual evidence.
points: Keep participant and quote references.
Look for exceptions and conflicting experiences.
State sample size, provenance and limitations.
slides.note: Prompt 18 supports qualitative synthesis. Theme frequency within a small sample does not establish population prevalence.

paragraphs: Qualitative synthesis needs traceability. Connect themes to participant references and actual quotes, include exceptions, and state the sample limitations. Repetition in a small sample can be informative without establishing population prevalence.
For SkillForge, two learners mentioning unclear prerequisites may justify a focused test. It does not establish what percentage of the entire market has that problem.
Choose one theme. Can you find its supporting evidence and a counterexample, or are you relying only on the AI summary?
Next, we will make the boundary between real and simulated interviews explicit.

slides.title: Synthetic interviews are for practice
slides.takeaway: Generated responses cannot validate customer needs.
points: Prompt 17 creates clearly labeled fictional transcripts.
Use them to rehearse coding and synthesis.
Use real research to justify product decisions.
slides.note: Synthetic learner interviews are only practice data. SkillForge's actual curriculum, LMS and pricing decisions require real learner or buyer evidence.

paragraphs: Synthetic interviews are useful for practicing analysis, not for validating customer needs. A model can create internally consistent answers that merely reflect the assumptions already present in the persona and PRD.

If we generate three SkillForge learner interviews, label every transcript and every resulting synthesis as fictional training material. Their apparent agreement does not prove demand or research saturation.
Where will you obtain actual learner evidence before turning a practice theme into a product commitment?
Now we will translate verified findings into backlog candidates.

slides.title: Findings become backlog candidates
slides.takeaway: Preserve the evidence link when writing a story.
points: State the user need and supporting source.
Add business value and acceptance criteria.
Keep unvalidated ideas in discovery.
slides.note: Prompt 19 produces four stories. A polished story is not inherently a priority; revisit product goals, research validity and delivery constraints.

paragraphs: A research-backed story should retain its evidence link. Identify the user need, supporting source, business or learning value, acceptance criteria, and validation status. A well-written story can still be the wrong priority.
For SkillForge, a feedback-turnaround story should be grounded in actual learner needs and realistic mentor capacity. If it comes only from a simulated interview, keep it as a discovery hypothesis.
What must be true for your proposed story to help the user, and what evidence do you have for that assumption?
Next, we will communicate the analysis as a decision memo.

slides.title: Your artifact: a decision memo
slides.takeaway: Explain enough for someone else to challenge the analysis.
points: Question, data scope and methods.
Findings, uncertainty and supporting tables.
Recommendation, next experiment and owner.
slides.note: Use prompts 15–19. The sample funnel CSV is fictional and defines visitors, leads, paid seats, activation and completed capstones. It includes tuition/refund and marketing inputs rather than real business results.

paragraphs: A decision memo helps someone else challenge your reasoning. State the question, scope, method, findings, limitations, recommendation, and next measurement. Make the evidence accessible without forcing the reader to repeat every calculation.

For SkillForge, the memo should connect learning quality with conversion, refunds, and contribution assumptions. Growing tuition revenue is not enough if learners fail to achieve the outcome or service costs exceed the value.
What is the clearest next decision from your analysis, and what uncertainty would you explicitly bring to the discussion?
Use the analytics prompts, inspect the fictional data, and record a recommendation that respects its limits.

modules.title: Strategic thinking & problem solving
modules.subtitle: Explore uncertainty, challenge assumptions and choose the next experiment.
objectives: Choose a strategic experiment and review the full portfolio.

slides.title: AI as a thought partner
slides.takeaway: Use analysis to expand and challenge your options.
points: Explore ideas and alternative explanations.
Plan around uncertainty and constraints.
Communicate the decision and its trade-offs.
slides.note: AI is not inherently unbiased. Ask for counterarguments and missing evidence, then apply domain judgment.

paragraphs: Use AI as a thought partner to expand and challenge your options. Ask for alternative explanations, trade-offs, and missing evidence. Then apply your domain knowledge and take responsibility for the choice.

SkillForge could improve curriculum clarity, add feedback capacity, or broaden acquisition. AI can help compare these paths, but our decision should depend on learning outcomes, evidence, and available resources.
Which strategic assumption are you currently treating as settled? Ask what evidence would make you reconsider it.
Next, we will connect the course funnel to commercial outcomes.

slides.title: Define the course revenue funnel
slides.takeaway: Interest, enrollment, completion and profit are different.
points: Visitors → qualified leads → paid seats, limited by capacity.
Gross tuition − refunds = net tuition.
Subtract acquisition, delivery, processing and fixed costs.
slides.note: The worked case uses an illustrative $299 seat price and 30-seat capacity. The revenue lab is an editable planning model, not a revenue forecast or a live checkout.

paragraphs: Interest, paid enrollment, course completion, and profit are different outcomes. Define the funnel and the cost model before interpreting the commercial story. Capacity also matters: demand beyond the available seats does not automatically become revenue.

SkillForge's model starts with visitors, lead conversion, and paid conversion, then caps seats at delivery capacity. It subtracts expected refunds, processing, delivery, acquisition, and fixed campaign costs.
Which cost or denominator is easiest to overlook in your own business case? Write it down before using the calculator.
Now we will compare plausible scenarios rather than treating one estimate as certain.

slides.title: Build three plausible futures
slides.takeaway: Scenarios organize uncertainty rather than eliminate it.
points: Conservative: binding constraints persist.
Central: current drivers progress.
Accelerated: enabling conditions improve faster.
slides.note: Prompt 20 models conservative, central and accelerated course-enrollment campaigns with explicit conversion and cost assumptions. Growth in the category is not proof that the base case will occur.

paragraphs: A scenario is a conditional future: if these assumptions hold, this is the result the model produces. Build alternatives around meaningful constraints and drivers. Identify the signals that would help distinguish them early.

In SkillForge's worked case, a more successful campaign can still end at thirty seats because mentor capacity is limited. If acquisition spend must rise to produce that traffic, the costs should change too.
Which assumption could make your central scenario fail, and what would you monitor before committing more resources?
Next, we will use historical transitions to ask better strategic questions.

slides.title: Use history with boundaries
slides.takeaway: A useful analogy includes where it breaks.
points: Identify similar incentives and infrastructure.
Compare switching costs, regulation and users.
Convert the lesson into a testable hypothesis.
slides.note: Prompt 21 explores bounded analogies in professional education. Cite evidence and explain where learner behavior, credentials, regulation or delivery economics differ.

paragraphs: Historical analogies can reveal useful patterns, but they should include where the comparison breaks. Consider audience, incentives, infrastructure, switching costs, and regulation. A similar-looking curve is not evidence that a new product will follow the same path.

For SkillForge, a transition from classroom learning to online delivery may suggest questions about flexibility and trust. It does not prove that a small reviewed-project course will gain the same adoption as a large platform.
What part of your analogy is genuinely similar, and what difference could overturn the lesson?
Now we will choose frameworks that fit the decision.

slides.title: Frameworks give analysis a shape
slides.takeaway: Ask a framework to clarify a specific decision.
points: Learning curves: performance versus cumulative experience.
Scenario planning: choices under uncertain futures.
Resource allocation: opportunity cost and constraints.
slides.note: Use a framework because it fits the problem. Merely naming one does not make the underlying evidence stronger.

paragraphs: A framework gives analysis a structure. Scenario planning organizes uncertainty; learning curves connect experience with performance; resource allocation makes opportunity cost explicit. Choose the framework because it clarifies your question, not because its name sounds rigorous.
For SkillForge, learning curves may help examine content-production effort, while the revenue model helps examine campaign viability. Neither framework validates learner demand on its own.
What question are you trying to answer, and which framework exposes the assumptions that matter most?
Next, we will apply learning curves to course operations.

slides.title: Learning curves in course operations
slides.takeaway: Improve efficiency without weakening the learning outcome.
points: Lesson production, exercise authoring and cohort onboarding.
Rubric grading, learner support and LMS operations.
Content maintenance measured against learning quality.
slides.note: Prompt 22 proposes seven applications. Measure cumulative experience against accepted output, not just content volume; preserve assessment standards and account for tool changes.

paragraphs: A learning curve needs a mechanism and a measure of cumulative experience. Improvements may also come from scale or technology changes, so keep those explanations separate. Add a quality guardrail so faster output is not mistaken for better work.
For SkillForge, track authoring hours per exercise that passes review, or support time per resolved learner issue. Producing more unchecked content would not demonstrate the improvement we want.
Choose one operational task. What output counts as acceptable, and what evidence would show that experience is helping?
Now we will turn strategic analysis into a small, reversible test.

slides.title: Choose a reversible strategic test
slides.takeaway: The next experiment should reduce decision uncertainty.
points: Compare options, upside, downside and reversibility.
Define a useful signal and stop/pivot threshold.
Name the owner and review date.
slides.note: Extension prompt 27 turns scenarios into a concrete experiment. Prompt 23 supports an interactive explanation when checkpoints are useful.

paragraphs: The next experiment should reduce uncertainty that affects a decision. Compare the options, define the earliest useful signal, and state success, stop, or pivot thresholds in advance. Name the owner and review point.

For SkillForge, a truthful pilot offer and a reviewed sample project can test more than an ambitious platform build. We need real evidence of commitment and learning value, together with actual delivery costs.
What is the smallest action that could change your launch decision, and what would you do if the result disappoints?
Next, we will review the entire product case as one connected story.

slides.title: Your capstone: an evidence-linked product story
slides.takeaway: Show how each artifact informs the next decision.
points: PRD → research → personas → prototype.
Roadmap → stories → priorities → analysis.
Scenario brief → experiment → next decision.
slides.note: Use prompt 28 and the course rubric. Review evidence, user relevance, traceability, feasibility, metrics and uncertainty rather than rewarding polished prose.

paragraphs: Your capstone is an evidence-linked product story. The PRD sets the direction, research challenges it, learner work informs the experience, and the roadmap and backlog explain execution. Analytics and strategy then shape the next experiment.

For SkillForge, check that the course promise matches its curriculum, the LMS supports the learner journey, and the revenue case includes delivery capacity and costs. Polish should not hide a broken connection.
Which artifact has the weakest evidence, and what is the most important improvement before making a real commitment?
Use the capstone review and final prompts. Finish by stating your next decision, its owner, and the evidence you still need.

stories.title: Understand the course before buying
stories.story: As a working analyst, I want outcomes, prerequisites, workload, syllabus, sample content and price in one place so I can decide whether this course fits.
stories.value: Reduce unsuitable purchases and improve qualified conversion.
criteria: The page shows eight weeks, 5–7 hours/week, Python/SQL prerequisites and assessment requirements.
The pilot price and refund conditions are visible before enrollment.
A sample lesson is accessible without a purchase; no placement or accreditation claim is implied.
stories.dependencies: Reviewed proposition, curriculum outline and commercial terms.

stories.title: Enroll with clear payment and access status
stories.story: As a learner, I want a reliable enrollment confirmation so I know whether I have paid and can access the course.
stories.value: Support paid conversion without duplicate charges or lost access.
criteria: Production uses a vetted payment provider and never stores raw card details in the LMS.
A successful provider event grants access once; duplicate events are idempotent.
Failed or pending payment shows recovery guidance; confirmation includes the purchase and refund details.
stories.dependencies: Identity/access roles, provider integration, approved terms and security review.

stories.title: Study an accessible lesson
stories.story: As a time-constrained learner, I want an accessible lesson with a transcript and practice so I can learn in my available study window.
stories.value: Support learning activation and a credible minimum product.
criteria: Lessons include an outcome, readable text, captioned media where used and a worked example.
All controls work with a keyboard and have visible focus and labels.
A network or content-loading error gives a retry path without losing progress.
stories.dependencies: Approved accessible content and authenticated course access.

stories.title: Resume where I stopped
stories.story: As a learner, I want the next unfinished lesson and my saved position so I can continue without searching.
stories.value: Reduce resumption friction and support weekly engagement.
criteria: The workspace identifies the last opened and next unfinished lesson.
Progress updates persist for the correct learner; learners cannot see another account's records.
Completion indicators distinguish viewed content from passed assessments.
stories.dependencies: Course structure, identity and a progress-event definition.

stories.title: Get feedback from a knowledge check
stories.story: As a learner, I want explanations and retries after a quiz so I can correct misunderstandings.
stories.value: Improve comprehension rather than rewarding clicks.
criteria: Each answer shows why it is correct or incorrect after submission.
Retry is allowed and does not overwrite the distinction between an attempt and a final passing result.
Question text, options and feedback are keyboard/screen-reader accessible.
stories.dependencies: Assessment blueprint, item review and scoring logic.

stories.title: Submit a project against a visible rubric
stories.story: As a learner, I want to submit a notebook or repository against clear criteria so I can demonstrate my learning.
stories.value: Create a credible learning artifact and capstone completion signal.
criteria: The rubric is visible before submission and covers analysis, validation, communication and responsible AI use.
Allowed link/file types and permissions are explained; malformed submissions show useful errors.
Submission receipt and status persist; resubmissions follow a published policy.
stories.dependencies: Project brief, submission storage/access controls and rubric.

stories.title: Receive actionable mentor feedback
stories.story: As a learner, I want rubric-level feedback so I know what to improve before final review.
stories.value: Test the feedback differentiator and improve completion quality.
criteria: Feedback links to rubric criteria with at least one strength and next action.
The promised turnaround is shown and supported by actual mentor capacity.
Only the learner and authorized reviewer can access private submissions and feedback.
stories.dependencies: LMS-06, reviewer roles and mentor staffing.

stories.title: Plan study time and office hours
stories.story: As a working learner, I want a weekly plan and clear office-hour times so I can schedule consistent practice.
stories.value: Reduce missed support and expectation mismatch.
criteria: The plan shows estimated work, due dates and time zone.
Office hours show availability and joining instructions.
Reminders are opt-in and can be disabled.

stories.title: Find help without losing context
stories.story: As a blocked learner, I want to ask a question from a lesson so I can recover and keep learning.
stories.value: Improve recovery and reveal costly recurring content issues.
criteria: The help request can include lesson context with learner permission.
A help page states response expectations and escalation.
Requests are acknowledged and visible only to permitted staff and the learner.
stories.dependencies: Support workflow, staffing and access controls.

stories.title: Understand completion and credential rules
stories.story: As a learner, I want clear completion criteria and a verifiable record so I understand what I have achieved.
stories.value: Support truthful outcomes communication and trust.
criteria: Completion requires the stated assessments and rubric threshold, not merely video views.
Any completion record states issuer and criteria without implying external accreditation.
Corrections or revoked records follow an explicit policy.
stories.dependencies: Assessment and completion policy; verified outcome records.

sections.title: 01 / Draft the course and LMS PRD
sections.intro: Problem hypothesis: some analysts struggle to connect scattered data-science and GenAI resources into a manageable project path with useful feedback. This must be checked with real learners.
points: Primary learner: a working analyst who can already use basic Python and SQL; an early-career learner is secondary, not a zero-to-expert promise.
Value proposition: a bounded eight-week sequence, a data project and a GenAI evaluation capstone, reviewed with a visible rubric.
MVP: an outcome-led course page, prerequisite check, enrollment/access, accessible lessons, progress, quizzes, project submission and staffed feedback.
Non-goals: accredited degree, guaranteed job placement, comprehensive advanced ML, enterprise SSO, a custom LMS engine or an unrestricted AI tutor.
Build/buy: begin on an existing LMS with proven access, payments, assignments and gradebook; customize the proposition and learning service before rebuilding commodity infrastructure.

Start with the provisional PRD. We are defining a course business and its delivery experience together: who it serves, what learning outcome it promises, and what must be true for that promise to be credible.

The roadmap connects research, curriculum readiness, platform configuration, and pilot delivery. Its gates matter more than how tidy the timeline looks.
A course can fail if marketing is ready before content and support. Review dependencies with the people responsible for instruction, implementation, and operations.
What evidence must be available at the next gate before you would release more budget?

Read the ten stories as candidates for refinement. Each should connect a user goal with business or learning value and testable behavior.

sections.title: 09 / Prioritize with RICE and release gates
sections.intro: Reach is the estimated number of learners, out of one planned 30-learner cohort, that a story would affect during a 90-day pilot window, so some stories reach 18 or 24 rather than all 30. Impact uses one agreed scale; confidence is a fraction in calculation; effort is person-months.
points: RICE = reach × impact × confidence ÷ effort. Scores are conversation inputs, not measured business facts.
Pilot path: course transparency, secure enrollment/access, reviewed lessons, progress, knowledge checks, submission and staffed feedback.
Mandatory gates override ranking: identity/access isolation, provider-backed payments, refund disclosure, accessibility, content review and sufficient mentor capacity.
The example scope consumes several person-months in aggregate. Configure existing LMS capabilities to fit the small-team constraint; re-estimate before committing.
sections.decision: Use the live RICE lab to test assumptions. Do not drop a prerequisite because its score is lower than a visible growth feature.

paragraphs: Step 9: Prioritize with RICE and release gates.
RICE makes assumed reach, impact, confidence, and effort visible. It does not replace the release checklist or the minimum coherent learner journey.
Use the ranking to ask why a story is near the top and what evidence supports its inputs. Then check required access controls, payments, content readiness, and feedback capacity.
Change one weak estimate in the live lab. Does the priority discussion change in a meaningful way?
Your next validation: Use the live RICE lab to test assumptions. Do not drop a prerequisite because its score is lower than a visible growth feature.

Revenue: gross tuition less full refunds. Track payment fees, mentor/platform cost and acquisition spend separately.

The practice data is fictional. It helps you rehearse a real analysis without pretending that a live course has produced these results.

Why Accelerated equals Central: demand of 80 seats is capped at the 30-seat delivery capacity, so tuition and contribution stop growing. Extra demand only pays off if capacity, mentors and spend change too.
The scenario table holds acquisition spend fixed for comparability, which may be unrealistic at higher traffic; change the inputs in the revenue lab.
This is an incremental planning model, not accounting profit: taxes, founder salary, ongoing overhead, chargebacks and additional content investment may be missing.
With these assumptions, per-seat contribution before fixed/acquisition costs is $221.11 and illustrative break-even is nine paid seats; ceiling and refund assumptions still matter.
sections.decision: Test the proposed price with an honestly described pilot offer. Track actual commitments and refunds; do not take payment before terms, delivery and support are ready.

paragraphs: Step 11: Plan revenue and validate willingness to pay.
This is a conditional revenue model. Gross tuition, net tuition, contribution, and accounting profit are different measures.

The central case fills thirty seats under explicit assumptions. The accelerated case does not sell beyond capacity, and higher traffic may require higher spend. Check the costs that the example excludes.
Open the calculator and change the assumption you trust least. Would you still launch the same pilot?
Your next validation: Test the proposed price with an honestly described pilot offer. Track actual commitments and refunds; do not take payment before terms, delivery and support are ready.

sections.title: 12 / Launch small, learn and revise
sections.intro: Recommended next step: a narrow paid-pilot validation, not a large LMS build or broad claim of market leadership.
points: Recruit 12 qualified learners plus three buyer interviews; record past purchase behavior and prerequisite readiness.
Publish a truthful offer and sample lesson. Define channel/measurement before running a small campaign.
Set the gate in advance: at least 10 qualified paid commitments with acceptable acquisition cost before completing full production; this threshold is a proposed test.
If interest is high but payment is low, investigate proposition and willingness to pay. If payment is healthy but completion is poor, fix learning/service quality before scaling.
Review activation, rubric completion, refunds, mentor load and contribution after the mature pilot; log the decision to iterate, stop or expand.

overview.title: Your trainer-led learning path
paragraphs: Welcome to Generative AI in Product Management. We will learn by developing SkillForge Academy, a fictional Data Science and Generative AI course business and LMS.

Work through six modules in order: define the product, investigate the market, understand learners, plan delivery, analyze evidence, and make strategic decisions. Each module gives you an artifact to review.
At any step, choose Listen to trainer for an explanation, example, reflection question, and next action. Use the transcript if you prefer reading, and pause whenever you need time to practice.
The voice uses your browser's available speech service. You control playback and speed. Begin with module one, or open the worked course case to see how the artifacts connect.

library.title: How to practice with a prompt
paragraphs: Use this reference to choose the task you actually need to do. The course-case version follows SkillForge Academy, and the reusable version uses your current product context.
Attach real approved source files, replace the context where needed, and run the prompt in a suitable AI tool. This website prepares prompts; it does not execute them.
Each prompt has its own trainer walkthrough and review checks. Judge the output by evidence, user relevance, and the decision it supports. Keep a record of which assumptions remain unvalidated.

rice.title: Coach me through RICE
paragraphs: Start by reading the time horizon and units. In this exercise, reach is the number of learners, out of a planned thirty-seat cohort, that a story would affect during a ninety-day pilot window, so some stories reach eighteen or twenty-four rather than thirty. Values are illustrative.

Change one input at a time and watch the score and ranking. Confidence is displayed as a percentage but divided by one hundred in the calculation. An empty or invalid effort should not produce a meaningful score.
Choose the top two candidates and ask which input is least supported. Then identify dependencies and required release controls that the numerical ranking does not capture.
Save your rationale. The goal is an explainable prioritization discussion, not merely the largest score.

data.title: Coach me through course analytics
paragraphs: Begin with the fictional-data label and cohort definition. This exercise assumes every cohort has completed its eight-week window. That matters when comparing completion.
Use the channel filter, inspect the table, and recalculate one total. Net tuition subtracts fully refunded seats from paid seats and uses the assumed tuition price.
Compare paid volume, activation, assessed completion, and acquisition spend. The second channel chart is labeled as an all-channel view.
Write an observation separately from its possible explanation, then state the next evidence or experiment you would need.

revenue.title: Coach me through the revenue model
paragraphs: Read the model as a set of assumptions. Visitors become leads, leads become paid seats, and delivery capacity caps the result. Expected refunds may be fractional even though seats are whole numbers.
The model subtracts refunds, processing on gross tuition, variable delivery, acquisition spend, and fixed campaign or content cost. It does not automatically include tax, salary, or every overhead.

Change the least certain conversion or cost input. Then check whether break-even is possible within capacity. If unit contribution is not positive, selling more seats will not solve the assumed economics.
Record which input needs real evidence before making a launch or expansion decision.

scenario.title: Coach me through scenarios
paragraphs: This explorer is an abstract adoption illustration rather than a course-sales forecast. Adoption means the share of a defined eligible learner audience taking a course.
Adjust the starting adoption, ceiling, growth parameter, and horizon. The model shows how different assumptions create different conditional outcomes.

Do not infer that any scenario is likely just because a curve looks smooth. Ask which leading indicator could help distinguish the futures. Use the separate revenue model for course conversion and costs.
Save the assumption you would test first and the decision it could change.

capstone.title: Coach me through the portfolio review
paragraphs: Review the full set of artifacts together: product definition, research, learners, curriculum, prototype, roadmap, stories, analytics, and strategic experiment.

Score evidence, user relevance, traceability, feasibility, metric quality, and uncertainty from zero to two. Zero means missing, one means partial or assumption-based, and two means clear and supported.
A high total is not certification. Focus on the weakest link that could change a real product decision.
Write three improvements and one next validation step, then export your portfolio so you can discuss it with your team.

lmsCatalog.title: Coach me through course discovery
paragraphs: Approach this screen as a prospective learner. Look for the learning outcome, prerequisite knowledge, workload, format, price hypothesis, and evidence of what you will be able to demonstrate.
Try searching the learning outcomes, inspect the syllabus, and preview the sample before deciding. Observe whether any purchase-relevant information is missing or hard to find.
The enrollment action is a local demonstration. It takes no payment and grants no real course access. Use it to investigate the interaction rather than to measure genuine buying intent.
Your task is to decide whether this course fits the intended learner, and to note any question that a real user would still need answered.

lmsLearning.title: Coach me through the learner workspace
paragraphs: Now follow the learner's main task. Read the sample explanation about evaluation and data leakage, then use the knowledge check to test your understanding.
Marking a lesson complete is different from demonstrating the learning outcome. Review the project rubric before saving a link, and notice the confirmation and error behavior.
The demo stores state and project links on this device. No mentor receives or grades the submission, and no credential is issued.
Observe whether a learner can resume, understand feedback, and recover from a mistake without help. That is the evidence this prototype can help you collect.

paragraphs: These downloads let you use the course outside the website. The prompt reference, the worked course case and the trainer transcript are ready to print or save.
Keep the prompt handbook and worked academic case alongside your own artifacts. Refer to linked sources and maintain their dates, populations, and limitations.
Audio on this site is browser speech, not a recording inside the downloaded files. Your learning notes remain on this device unless you export them.
